samples.summary: Session/refresh cookie `Secure` flag silently downgraded from `NODE_ENV` to a derivation of `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`
samples.evidence: `baseCookieOptions()` previously returned `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'`; it now returns `secure: secureCookies(this.configService)` (auth.controller.ts:536), which resolves through `github-auth.guard.ts:158-171` to `false` whenever `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` starts with `http://` — regardless of `NODE_ENV`. A perfectly functional production deployment that terminates TLS at an edge and has a GitHub OAuth app whose callback URL is registered as `http://app.example.com/auth/github/callback` (GitHub permits http callback URLs, and an http→https edge redirect preserves the query so the flow still works) previously got `Secure` session and refresh cookies and now gets them without `Secure`. The tokens are then sent in cleartext on any http request to the origin an active network attacker can induce, yielding full session theft. The only signal is a single `logger.warn` (`warnIfPlainHttpProduction`, github-auth.guard.ts:106-117) at first login; nothing fails, and an existing deployment upgrading to this build receives no configuration change prompt. `COOKIE_SECURE=true` exists as an opt-out but must be discovered. This is a real security-relevant regression for the *session* token (a long-lived credential), even though the same derivation is well justified for the 5-minute login bindings.

samples.summary: Login-binding cookie ring is evictable cross-site: an attacker page can force a victim's in-flight login to be refused
samples.evidence: `issueLoginCookie` (github-auth.guard.ts:647-666) appends a fresh binding to a ring bounded at `MAX_CONCURRENT_LOGINS = 3`, dropping the oldest (`.slice(-(MAX_CONCURRENT_LOGINS - 1))`, line 658). `GET /auth/github` is unauthenticated and has no per-route throttle (only the global 120/min in app.module.ts:100), so any third-party page can issue three cross-site subresource requests (``) whose responses each carry a `Set-Cookie` for `wafflebase_oauth_state` / `wafflebase_cli_confirm`. The victim's genuine in-flight binding is evicted and their callback then fails the check, landing them on `/login?error=login_state` — or, for the CLI, re-rendering the consent page forever. Same effect via a second vector: `takeStateCookie` (auth.controller.ts:367-370) clears the *entire* ring when nothing matches, and an attacker holding a GitHub authorization code for their own account can navigate the victim to `/auth/github/callback?code=&state=` to trigger it. Impact is denial-of-login, not credential compromise; browsers that block third-party cookie *setting* mitigate the first vector.

samples.summary: CLI-login plain-http exemption keys on the configured callback URL's host, not on the origin actually being served
samples.evidence: `cliLoginAvailable` (github-auth.guard.ts:215-217) returns true when `loopbackCallback(configService)` is true, i.e. when `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`'s hostname is `localhost`/`127.0.0.0/8`/`[::1]` (lines 181-194). That is a configuration string, not the origin the request arrived on. The sample env shipped in `packages/backend/README.md` is exactly `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL=http://localhost:3000/auth/github/callback`. A self-hosted install that leaves that line as-is while exposing the backend on a routable http origin therefore enables `?mode=cli` with a `wafflebase_cli_confirm` cookie that is NOT `__Host-` prefixed (secureCookies → false → bare name, line 238) — precisely the plantable-cookie condition the `400 Command-line sign-in requires an https server` refusal exists to prevent, and the consent page naming the loopback port would never be shown to the person it protects. Mitigating: such a deployment's GitHub redirect would also point at localhost, so the browser flow would be broken too — which limits, but does not eliminate, the window (e.g. a deployment mid-migration, or a GHE setup where the authorization URL is overridden).

samples.summary: CLI writes live login secrets (nonce + PKCE challenge) to disk via a delete-then-write sequence that follows symlinks and survives abnormal exit
samples.evidence: `announceLoginUrl` (login.ts:212-243) writes the full authorization URL — which carries this login's `nonce` and `code_challenge`, the two bindings the loopback flow rests on — to `~/.wafflebase/login-url.txt`. The sequence is `rmSync(file, {force:true})` (line 227) then `writeFileSync(file, ..., {mode: 0o600})` (line 228). `writeFileSync` follows symlinks, so anything able to create a path at that name between the two calls redirects the write (and, more usefully to an attacker, could pre-place a symlink to a file they can read, harvesting the secrets). The containing directory is created with `mkdirSync(..., {recursive:true})` (line 224) at the default umask-derived mode (typically 0755), so it is world-traversable. Deletion happens only in the `finally` at login.ts:82; a SIGKILL or a crash leaves the live URL on disk for the full five-minute server TTL. Using `writeFileSync(file, url, {mode:0o600, flag:'wx'})` (or an `O_NOFOLLOW` open) would close the symlink window.

samples.summary: The state-bearing `GET /auth/github` redirect sets a login cookie with no `Cache-Control: no-store`, unlike the consent page
samples.evidence: The CLI consent response explicitly carries `Cache-Control: no-store` (auth.controller.ts:144) because it embeds a single-use confirm token. The *other* half of the same mechanism — the 302 to GitHub whose `Location` carries `state` and whose `Set-Cookie` carries the matching binding (issued at github-auth.guard.ts:661, state assembled at 589) — carries no cache directives at all. A 302 is not heuristically cacheable by a conformant shared cache without explicit freshness, so this is defence-in-depth rather than a live bug, but any CDN/edge configured to cache 3xx (some are, for redirect offload) would hand two different browsers the same login binding, letting one complete the other's login. I searched auth.controller.ts, github-auth.guard.ts, main.ts and app.module.ts for any global header middleware or helmet — there is none, so nothing else supplies it.

samples.summary: `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` is used raw with no length or entropy floor
samples.evidence: `bindingSecret` returns any truthy `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` verbatim (github-auth.guard.ts:335-336), skipping the HKDF path entirely. `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET=x` is accepted and becomes the HMAC key for both `stateSignature` and `consentToken` — and, as the file's own comment notes, one unauthenticated `GET /auth/github` publishes a verified (input, MAC) pair under that key, making an offline key search trivial against a short value. The empty-string case is handled correctly (`||` in the `JWT_SECRET` path, line 343) but the dedicated-secret path has no equivalent floor. A minimum-length check (or the same `||` fallback) at line 336 would make 'set but useless' fail like 'unset'. I grepped for OAUTH_STATE_SECRET across packages/backend/src and the docs; the only validation is truthiness here.
searchedFor: grep for a config validation schema / Joi in packages/backend/src

samples.summary: `stateSignature` and `consentToken` share one HMAC key with no domain-separation tag
samples.evidence: Both `stateSignature` (github-auth.guard.ts:374-376, message = the raw cookie value) and `consentToken` (409-423, message = length-prefixed `cookie|port|nonce|challenge`) are HMAC-SHA256 under the same `bindingSecret`. I traced whether one output can be replayed as the other and it cannot today: the only values ever fed to `stateSignature` are server-generated 43-char base64url cookie values, which can never equal a `consentToken` preimage (that starts `43:` and is much longer), and the cookie ring is server-written and `__Host-`-protected. So this is currently safe *by accident of the value space*, not by construction. Prefixing each message with a distinct constant tag (e.g. `state|` vs `consent|`) would make the separation structural and survive a future change to what gets signed.

verdict.reason: The described code exists verbatim: baseCookieOptions() sets `secure: secureCookies(this.configService)` (auth.controller.ts:536) for both the session and refresh cookies (auth.controller.ts:484-498, 473-477), and secureCookies() returns false for any `http://` GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL irrespective of NODE_ENV (github-auth.guard.ts:162-169), with NODE_ENV only as a no-callback-URL fallback (line 170). The only mitigation in the downgrade path is a once-per-process logger.warn (github-auth.guard.ts:106-117) — log-only, nothing fails closed — and COOKIE_SECURE (lines 80-89) is opt-in configuration an upgrading deployment gets no prompt to set, so it is not a guard that makes the weakness unreachable. No compensating control exists: the code itself notes there is no helmet/global header layer (auth.controller.ts:136; auth.controller.spec.ts:648), so no HSTS, and `trust proxy` (main.ts:39-41) is unrelated. A TLS-terminating deployment whose registered GitHub callback URL is http:// therefore transmits a long-lived session/refresh credential without `Secure`, exposing it to an active network attacker who induces any plain-http request to the origin — sensitive credential exposure, squarely in the security lane, major impact.

finding.summary: The session and refresh cookies still carry no `__Host-`/`__Secure-` prefix, so even with `secureCookies()===true` a sibling subdomain can plant `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` — the protection the new comment claims for 'a cookie worth stealing' covers only the `Secure` flag
finding.evidence: `baseCookieOptions` (auth.controller.ts:534-538) returns `{httpOnly, secure, sameSite}` and `setAuthCookies` writes the fixed names `wafflebase_session` / `wafflebase_refresh` (lines 59-60, 484, 492) with no prefix and no `path`. Grep for `__Host-` across packages shows the prefix is applied only in `loginCookieName` (github-auth.guard.ts:238); no session cookie ever gets it. The guard's own reasoning (github-auth.guard.ts:222-232) is that without the prefix any sibling subdomain or anything able to inject a `Set-Cookie` for the registrable domain can write the cookie — applied to the session cookie that is session fixation: an attacker plants their own valid access/refresh token, the victim's browser sends it on every request, and the victim's work lands in the attacker's account. This delta's new comment (lines 527-533) asserts the session cookie's exposure is now handled by `COOKIE_SECURE` + the warning, which addresses only the transport flag, not cookie planting. Pre-existing code, raised because the delta reasons explicitly about this cookie's threat model.

verdict.reason: The absence claim holds. Session/refresh cookies are written with the bare literal names ACCESS_COOKIE_NAME='wafflebase_session' / REFRESH_COOKIE_NAME='wafflebase_refresh' (auth.controller.ts:59-60) via setAuthCookies (auth.controller.ts:484,492) and clearAuthCookies (auth.controller.ts:475-476), with baseCookieOptions (auth.controller.ts:515-539) returning only {httpOnly, secure, sameSite} — no prefix, no path. A repo-wide grep for __Host-/__Secure- (all packages, docs, scripts, tests, node_modules excluded as irrelevant) shows the only production application is github-auth.guard.ts:238 inside loginCookieName, reached solely for the three short-lived login cookies (oauth_state, cli_state, cli_confirm; see github-auth.guard.spec.ts:687,730,761). The read paths confirm the unprefixed name is authoritative and there is no prefixed fallback: jwt.strategy.ts:13 reads request?.cookies?.wafflebase_session and auth.controller.ts:428 reads req.cookies?.[REFRESH_COOKIE_NAME]. No indirect rewrite exists — main.ts:64 installs plain cookieParser() with no prefix logic and there is no global cookie middleware. The project's own design doc corroborates: docs/design/backend.md:382-384 lists session/refresh as unprefixed while only wafflebase_oauth_state is __Host-prefixed, and docs/design/backend.md:404-408 asserts __Host- is 'the only thing' that stops a sibling subdomain writing a cookie. Applying that same stated threat model to the session cookie yields cookie planting / session fixation: an attacker who can set a cookie for the registrable domain plants their own valid access/refresh token, jwt.strategy.ts:13 consumes it, and the victim's work lands in the attacker's account. The Secure flag reasoned about in the new comment (auth.controller.ts:527-533) addresses transport only, not planting. In-lane (auth/session integrity) and not already guarded anywhere I could find.

finding.summary: Session/refresh cookie `Secure` flag is now derived from `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`'s scheme, so a misconfigured `http://` callback on a TLS-fronted deployment silently drops `Secure` from the session token
finding.evidence: `baseCookieOptions()` changed from `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'` to `secure: secureCookies(this.configService)` (auth.controller.ts:528). `secureCookies` (github-auth.guard.ts:91-98) returns `false` for *any* `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` starting with `http://`, and that branch is checked before the `NODE_ENV==='production'` fallback. Previously a production deployment always got `Secure` session/refresh cookies regardless of that variable. Now a deployment that terminates TLS at a proxy and leaves `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL=http://...` (the exact spelling the self-hosting guide prints, packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:121) serves `wafflebase_session` / `wafflebase_refresh` without `Secure` on an https site — the JWT then rides any plaintext request to the origin and is trivially stolen by a network attacker or a downgrade link. The reasoning in the comment (a Secure cookie on an http origin is dropped) is sound for a genuinely-http origin, but the predicate reads a config string, not the actual serving scheme, so one wrong env value silently removes a transport control from the session cookie rather than only from the 5-minute login cookie. Consider keeping `secure: true` whenever `NODE_ENV==='production'` OR the callback is https, and only relaxing for loopback.

verdict.reason: The mechanism is present as described, though the cited line numbers are off and the "silently" framing is inaccurate. auth.controller.ts:536 sets the session/refresh cookies with `secure: secureCookies(this.configService)`. github-auth.guard.ts:158-171 (not 91-98) returns false for any `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` starting with `http://` (line 166-169), and that branch is evaluated before the `NODE_ENV === 'production'` fallback (line 170). So a TLS-terminating deployment that leaves a stale `http://` callback URL serves `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` without `Secure` on an https origin — a real weakening of a transport control on a bearer session JWT, and self-hosting.md:121 does hand out an `http://` callback spelling. I could not refute on `already-guarded`: the two mitigations I found — the `COOKIE_SECURE` override checked first (github-auth.guard.ts:80-89, 159-160) and the production warning (github-auth.guard.ts:106-117) — both require operator action and do not make the unsafe path unreachable; they only make it non-silent and documented (self-hosting.md:133-139). Since the weakness is real, in-lane (sensitive data exposure / weakened cookie transport control), and not unreachable, the finding stands; confidence is low only because the override + warning + documentation substantially reduce its practical blocking weight, and the alternative the reviewer proposes would set `Secure` on genuinely-http origins where the browser discards the cookie entirely.
